web/sessions/routes/composer/guided.py:R: R6 `except GuidedOperationSettlementConflictError:` around `service.settle_guided_state_operation(...)` in POST /guided/reenter. Not a swallow: the handler's body is `failed = await service.fail_guided_operation(reserved.fence, failure_code='stale_conflict', ...)` followed by `raise_guided_operation_failure(failed)`, which is annotated `-> Never` and whose every exit is a raise (verified by reading its body: `raise AuditIntegrityError(...)` for an unknown code, otherwise `raise HTTPException(status_code=status_code, detail=body)`). `_handler_is_silent` fires purely because the raise is one call frame away — the rule scans the handler's own scope for an `ast.Raise` node, so a delegated terminal raise is invisible to it. The conflict is also durably recorded before the HTTP failure: `fail_guided_operation` settles the reserved fence as terminally failed with `failure_code='stale_conflict'`, so a lost CAS race is an audited operation outcome, not a dropped error. Inlining the raise would duplicate the closed `_SAFE_FAILURES` status/detail table that `raise_guided_operation_failure` deliberately single-owns. The caught exception is Tier-1: `GuidedOperationSettlementConflictError` is a `RuntimeError` subclass declared in `web/sessions/protocol.py` and raised only by ELSPETH's own session service. Control: `raise_guided_operation_failure` (Never-returning, in `web/sessions/routes/guided_operations.py`) plus `SessionServiceProtocol.fail_guided_operation`.

R6 `except GuidedOperationFenceLostError:` inside `post_guided_start`'s settlement retry loop. The handler's body is `continue`, and that IS the explicit outcome: losing the leader fence means another request won the cold-start takeover, so this attempt must leave the compose lock and rejoin through `reserve_or_replay_guided_operation`, which either observes the winner's completed operation and replays its response or performs the sole takeover. The loop's own comment states the invariant ('Never poll while holding the compose lock'). `_handler_is_silent` counts only `raise`, a non-default `return`, and a non-default `yield`, so a `continue` is invisible to it — and per the R4/R6 asymmetry entry in `docs/agents/recent-code-hints.md` (2026-08-29) a handler ending in `break`/`continue` cannot be extracted into a non-default-returning helper at all, because the control flow belongs to the enclosing loop. The loop cannot spin silently: its fall-through raises `AuditIntegrityError('Guided START settlement loop exited without a result')`. Tier-1 exception (`RuntimeError` subclass in `web/sessions/protocol.py`, raised only by our own service against our own fence rows). Control: the enclosing loop's `reserve_or_replay_guided_operation` rejoin plus that terminal `AuditIntegrityError`.

R4 `except Exception as exc:` — the terminal-failure handler of `post_guided_start`'s settlement attempt. Broad by design: every failure of a reserved guided cold-start operation must settle that operation's fence before any response leaves, or the session keeps a reserved-but-unsettled operation that blocks every later start. The handler classifies (`GuidedOperationSettlementConflictError` -> `stale_conflict`, `AuditIntegrityError` -> `integrity_error`, else `operation_failed`), logs integrity failures via `_safe_frame_strings` (documented and verified to emit only `file:line:function` — never source text, locals, or exception values), calls `service.fail_guided_operation`, and ends in `raise_guided_operation_failure(failed)`, whose every exit is a raise. Per the recent-code-hints R4/R6 asymmetry entry, the R4 arm scans only for `ast.Raise` in the handler's own scope, so a delegated terminal raise cannot clear it; narrowing the caught set would merely convert this into an R6 at the same line while dropping the fence settlement for every class it stopped catching — strictly worse. Note `BaseException` is deliberately NOT caught here: `asyncio.CancelledError` has its own preceding handler with distinct settlement semantics. Control: `raise_guided_operation_failure` (Never) and `SessionServiceProtocol.fail_guided_operation`; diagnostic redaction by `_safe_frame_strings` and `_failure_log_request_id`.

R6 `except GuidedOperationFenceLostError: continue` nested inside `post_guided_start`'s broad terminal handler, guarding the `service.fail_guided_operation` call. Losing the fence while recording the failure means another request already took the operation over and owns its terminal state, so this attempt must not raise its own HTTP failure over the winner's outcome — `continue` returns to the retry loop, where `reserve_or_replay_guided_operation` observes the winner and replays its authoritative response. Writing a second terminal failure against a fence we no longer hold is exactly the write the service layer refuses. As with the sibling `continue` handler above, extraction into a returning helper is impossible because the control flow belongs to the enclosing loop, whose fall-through `AuditIntegrityError` is the fail-closed backstop. Tier-1 exception. Control: the enclosing loop's `reserve_or_replay_guided_operation` rejoin and its terminal `AuditIntegrityError`.

R4 `except Exception as exc:` — the terminal-failure handler of `post_guided_convert` (POST /guided/convert, freeform -> guided). Structurally identical to the `post_guided_start` handler and broad for the same reason: the fence reserved for this conversion must be settled on every failure path or the session keeps an unsettled operation. It classifies into the same three closed codes, logs `AuditIntegrityError` with `_safe_frame_strings` + `_failure_log_request_id`, awaits `service.fail_guided_operation`, and ends in `raise_guided_operation_failure(failed)`, whose every exit is a raise. R4 fires because the terminating raise is delegated rather than lexically inside the handler; narrowing the caught tuple would convert it to an R6 at the same line and leave the un-caught classes abandoning a reserved fence. Control: `raise_guided_operation_failure` (Never) plus `SessionServiceProtocol.fail_guided_operation`.

R5 `isinstance(option, Mapping)` in `_schema8_permitted_plugins`, reading each entry of a single-select turn's `payload['options']`. Kept as the ABC form on ADR-032 Tier-3 grounds rather than on a container-identity claim, and the distinction matters because I measured the identity question and it does NOT support conversion-by-necessity: both producers of this value yield exact `dict` today (`_load_durable_current_turn` applies `dict(deep_thaw(prepared.payload))`, and `_finalize_guided_turn` applies `dict(deep_thaw(turn['payload']))` on the prospective path). What makes this a justify rather than a conversion is the value's TRUST DOMAIN, not its current concrete type: the payload is persisted to a content-addressed store and read back, which W3-6 and the neighbouring `routes/composer/proposals.py` prior art treat as Tier-3 on read-back, and ADR-032 prescribes the maximally-informative parse for a shape ELSPETH does not control at the point of read. The same key is adjudicated the same way one layer down: `web/composer/guided/protocol.py::_validate_options` (reached from `validate_current_turn`) validates each option through `_exact_nested_mapping`, an ABC-shaped check, under the module's declared boundaries. Narrowing here would put this route's read in conflict with the validator that certifies the same bytes, for no gain. Fail-closed polarity: a non-Mapping option raises `InvariantError('single-select turn contains a malformed option')`, which `post_guided_respond._preflight_or_sanitize` converts into the closed 500 envelope — it never abstains. The R1 half of this same line WAS removed in this lane (`option.get('id')` -> `'id' in option and option['id']`). Pinned by tests/integration/web/composer/guided/test_respond_schema8_atomic.py (single-select dispatch and durable-turn replay cases).

R5 `isinstance(edited['options'], Mapping)` in `_schema8_require_runnable_sink_form`'s closed-shape pre-check. This is the one site in the file where the ABC form is load-bearing for a MEASURED reason rather than a doctrinal one, and the reason is the gate's POLARITY. The `if` body is `return  # closed-shape violations are the transition contract's to reject`, so a False test ABSTAINS — it skips the deployment sink-admission check (`_schema8_require_runnable_sink_options`: the S2 sink-path allowlist and the file-sink collision-policy rule) rather than rejecting. An abstain gate is the silently-disabled polarity of W3-1, so narrowing it can only ever fail OPEN. And the narrowing is reachable, measured directly: `GuidedRespondRequest.model_validate({..., 'edited_values': {'plugin': 'csv', 'options': MappingProxyType({'path': 'a.csv'})}}, strict=True).edited_values['options']` is a `mappingproxy` — pydantic types `edited_values` as `dict[str, Any]` and passes its NESTED values through by identity, so a non-dict Mapping reaches this line from any in-process caller (the chat lane calls this same helper through `_schema8_answer_and_project_next`). Under `type(...) is dict` such a body would skip deployment sink admission entirely and admit a non-runnable sink into reviewed authority — reviewed sink options are fixed facts no planner repair may change, so admitting one guarantees planning later dies at REPAIR_EXHAUSTED with no user-visible cause (the elspeth-859e2702dd layer-3/4 defect this gate exists to prevent). Honest scope note: I did not find a PRODUCTION caller that passes a non-dict Mapping today — the chat lane's `_transition_request` builds `options` as `dict(deep_thaw(output.options))` — so this is a latent fail-open, not a live one. It stays ABC because the cost of being wrong is a silently skipped security-relevant admission check. Value tier: Tier-3 (client- or LLM-authored request body). Authoritative rejection of the same shape happens separately in `_schema8_transition`.

R5 `isinstance(options, Mapping)` in `_schema8_transition`'s SCHEMA_FORM arm — the authoritative reject-gate for the client-authored `edited_values['options']` (`if type(plugin) is not str or not isinstance(options, Mapping): raise ValueError('schema_form plugin and options have invalid types')`). Note the deliberate split on one line, which is the house structural-container / nominal-element shape recorded in recent-code-hints: the scalar `plugin` takes the exact-type form, the container takes the ABC. (2) Reachability of a non-dict Mapping is measured and real for in-process callers (see the `_schema8_require_runnable_sink_form` entry — pydantic preserves a nested `MappingProxyType` by identity), so narrowing would newly raise on bodies the sibling gate is written to accept, and the guided chat lane's degrade path would report the LLM's valid options as a turn-contract violation. Honest scope note: every production producer yields an exact `dict` today (HTTP JSON, and the chat lane's `dict(deep_thaw(...))`), so this is consistency and defence in depth, not a live break. Fail-closed polarity (raises).

R7 `with contextlib.suppress(Exception):` wrapping ONLY the two `slog.warning` emits inside `_preflight_attempt`'s turn-contract rejection handler. Best-effort telemetry around a diagnostic log, adjudicated against the operator-SIGNED precedent `web/composer/telemetry_phase8.py` (per-file R4 `pattern:` entry in `config/cicd/enforce_tier_model/web.yaml`): a structured-logging backend outage must not convert a well-defined HTTP 400 into a 500 the client cannot act on. Per the recent-code-hints guidance for these emitters, the check for whether a `TIER_1_ERRORS` re-raise arm is needed is whether the protected region contains an owned call that could raise a programmer error — here it does not: `scrub_text_for_audit`, the `.value` / `type(...).__name__` reads, and the class-constant `WebSurfacePolicyRejectedError.rejection_code` are all evaluated as arguments, and the region's own statement is the emit. The outcome is never lost: the next statement, OUTSIDE the suppress, is the unconditional `raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail='Guided response does not satisfy the current turn contract.') from exc`, so the rejection always reaches the client whether or not the log line was written. Control: that unconditional `raise HTTPException`.

R5 `isinstance(exc, WebSurfacePolicyRejectedError)` — the log-redaction discriminator inside the same turn-contract rejection handler. A justify candidate, not a conversion candidate, because the hierarchy is OPEN: `WebSurfacePolicyRejectedError` subclasses `ValueError` precisely so every existing client-fault catch admits it unchanged (its own docstring says so), and the enclosing `except (PluginConfigError, TypeError, ValueError)` catches the whole family. `type(exc) is WebSurfacePolicyRejectedError` would route any future subclass down the ELSE arm — the arm that deliberately WITHHOLDS `exc_message` — so the operator would silently lose the policy explanation for exactly the refusals this branch exists to surface, with no test failure to show for it. This is the same open-hierarchy exception-classifier shape that recent-code-hints records for `PlannerDeclined`/`PipelinePlannerError`. The discrimination is a REDACTION decision, not an admission gate: the True arm logs `scrub_text_for_audit(str(exc))` because that message is server-composed end to end (plugin name from the persisted turn's own permitted set, explanation from the policy predicate), while the False arm logs the exception CLASS only, because a generic contract message echoes raw client-supplied values (pinned by test_unsupported_guided_selection_never_reaches_operator_logs) and the audit scrubber redacts secret-SHAPED text, not arbitrary client text. Erring toward the False arm is safe; erring toward True would leak client text into operator logs. Value tier: the exception is Tier-1 ELSPETH-raised, but its MESSAGE carries Tier-3 client text on the generic branch, which is precisely what the split protects. Pinned by tests/integration/web/composer/guided/test_respond_schema8_atomic.py (asserts `rejection['exc_class'] == 'WebSurfacePolicyRejectedError'`).

R7 `with contextlib.suppress(Exception):` wrapping ONLY the `slog.error('guided.invariant_violated', ...)` emit in `_preflight_or_sanitize`. Same best-effort-telemetry disposition and same signed precedent as the sibling suppress above: a logging-backend failure must not replace the closed 500 invariant envelope with an uncontrolled exception raised from the error path itself. The one owned call in the region, `_safe_frame_strings(exc)`, is total over any `BaseException` by construction — it walks `__traceback__`/`__cause__` with an id-based cycle guard and a `max_frames` bound and formats only `file:line:function` — so there is no owned programmer error for a `TIER_1_ERRORS` arm to re-raise and such an arm would be dead code. The outcome is unconditional: the statement immediately after the suppress raises `HTTPException(status_code=500, detail={'error_type': 'server_invariant_violated', ...}) from exc`, so the invariant violation always terminates the request and is always visible to the client as the closed envelope. Control: that unconditional `raise HTTPException`.

R6 `except GuidedOperationFenceLostError:` in `post_guided_respond`'s settlement block; the handler's body is `rejoin_after_lock = True`. Not a swallow — that assignment IS the explicit outcome, consumed unconditionally by the `if rejoin_after_lock:` block immediately after the compose lock is released, which calls `reserve_or_replay_guided_operation` to observe the winner and replay its authoritative response, or raises `AuditIntegrityError('Guided RESPOND fence was lost without a joinable winner')` when no winner exists. The flag exists rather than an inline rejoin because the rejoin must NOT run while holding the session compose lock; re-raising here would abandon a completed sibling operation's result and return an error for work that actually succeeded. `_handler_is_silent` counts only `raise` / non-default `return` / non-default `yield`, so a flag consumed by the enclosing scope is structurally invisible to it. Tier-1 exception (`RuntimeError` subclass in `web/sessions/protocol.py`). Control: the `if rejoin_after_lock:` rejoin block and its terminal `AuditIntegrityError`.

R7 `with contextlib.suppress(Exception):` around the `slog.error('guided.operation_terminal_failure', ...)` emit in `post_guided_respond`'s broad terminal handler. Best-effort telemetry on the error path, same signed precedent (`web/composer/telemetry_phase8.py`) and same reasoning as the two suppresses above: the request is already failing, and the remaining work — settling the reserved fence via `fail_guided_operation_with_audit` and raising the closed HTTP envelope — must not be pre-empted by a logging backend fault. The owned calls in the region are `_safe_frame_strings` (total by construction, see above) and `_failure_log_request_id` (a membership-guarded read of `request.scope['state']` that returns `None` rather than probing, written for exactly this lenience — R2-F16b), so no owned programmer error can originate inside and a `TIER_1_ERRORS` re-raise arm would be dead code. The failure is never lost: the fence settlement and `raise_guided_operation_failure(failed)` follow unconditionally outside the suppress. Control: `service.fail_guided_operation_with_audit` plus the Never-returning `raise_guided_operation_failure`.

R6 `except GuidedOperationFenceLostError:` guarding `service.fail_guided_operation_with_audit` inside `post_guided_respond`'s broad terminal handler; body is `rejoin_after_lock = True`. Losing the fence while recording the terminal failure means another request took the operation over and owns its outcome, so this attempt must not raise its own envelope over the winner's — it sets the flag and lets the post-lock `if rejoin_after_lock:` block replay the winner's authoritative response, or raise `AuditIntegrityError` if there is none. Writing a second terminal failure against a fence we no longer hold is precisely the write the service layer refuses. Same rule blind spot as its sibling above: a flag consumed by the enclosing scope is neither a `raise` nor a `return` and so reads as silent. Tier-1 exception. Control: the `if rejoin_after_lock:` rejoin and its terminal `AuditIntegrityError`.

R7 `with contextlib.suppress(Exception):` around the `slog.error('guided.operation_failure_record_failed', ...)` emit — the innermost, last-resort diagnostic, reached only when recording the terminal failure ITSELF failed for a reason other than a lost fence. Suppressing here is what guarantees the handler reaches its own explicit outcome: the statement immediately after is `raise AuditIntegrityError('Guided RESPOND could not record its terminal failure') from None`, the fail-closed signal that audit custody was not established. Letting a logging-backend fault escape at this exact point would replace that precise integrity signal with an unrelated exception from the log call — the one place in the route where the audit-trail-gap diagnosis would be destroyed. The `from None` is deliberate: it keeps the failure-recording exception's text (which can quote service-layer detail) out of the raised chain. The region's only owned call is the total `_safe_frame_strings`. Control: the unconditional `raise AuditIntegrityError` on the next line.
